Genomic safety claims rested mainly on the absence of known lysogeny, resistance, and virulence genes, and functional transduction assays were largely absent. Ecuadorian bacteriophage research has begun to shift from demonstrating lysis toward molecularly defined products, but translational readiness is limited by fragmented publication, geographic concentration, and incomplete characterization. Decentralized laboratory capacity, national phage collections with deposited genomes, and standardized characterization pipelines would strengthen the field.

paper_title: Generative AI in Construction Safety: A Systematic Literature Review of Methods, Evidence, Deployment Gaps, and Future Directions
paper_abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being explored for construction safety; however, its maturity and practical reliability remain unclear. This study systematically reviews GenAI applications in construction safety and assesses whether existing evidence supports reliable, source-grounded, human-supervised, and deployable applications. The review followed a predefined protocol and PRISMA 2020. Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar were searched in May 2026 for studies published from 2019 to August 2026. After duplicate removal and screening, sixty-five studies were included. Data on GenAI methods, safety applications, validation, deployment, and limitations were extracted and synthesized thematically. Six application areas were identified: safety knowledge retrieval and decision support; incident report analysis and risk prediction; multimodal hazard reasoning; synthetic data generation; worker-centered training, communication and behavior support; and generative optimization, monitoring, and safety control. Several studies provided proof-of-concept evidence using historical datasets, simulations, laboratory experiments, or expert assessments, while evidence of generalizability, field deployment, hazard-exposure reduction, and incident prevention remained limited. GenAI showed potential to support hazard recognition, decision support, and compliance-related safety tasks, but field validation, source grounding, and integration with preventive controls are needed for reliable deployment. A conceptual framework linking GenAI capabilities, and preventive safety controls is proposed.

paper_title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
paper_abstract: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured.   Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint.   Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept.   Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size.   Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score.   Data Availability: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127920

paper_title: PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews
paper_abstract: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.

paper_title: ReviewPilot: A Multi-Agent System for Screening and Data Extraction in Systematic Reviews
paper_abstract: Systematic literature reviews follow the PRISMA process of screening scholarly works and extracting evidence from included studies. Deep research tools based on large language models (LLMs) can search and summarize the literature but do not record which studies are excluded or where extracted values come from. We develop a conversational multi-agent system called ReviewPilot that automates the PRISMA workflow from paper screening to information extraction. Researchers can tailor criteria and schemas through dialogue, and a project memory keeps their configurations and revisions. Each screening decision comes with its reason and each extracted value with its source. On epidemiological expert reviews, ReviewPilot outperforms a single-prompt LLM and AgentSLR across three LLMs, with screening macro F1 up to 0.776 and extraction F1 up to 0.788. Case studies in biomedicine and human-computer interaction show close agreement with human annotators, suggesting that ReviewPilot can transfer beyond epidemiology. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhaoqianXue/ReviewPilot.

paper_title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints. We separate the Modality Gap in cross-modal correspondence and evidence use from the Intent Gap in behavior relative to specified constraints, goals, and human expectations. Six dimensions organize the review: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. The first four control evidence access, optimization targets, supervision, and updates. Comparing mechanisms and supervision assumptions shows what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment. Evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels tests these choices through controlled input changes and reward-model validation, and we interpret each gain together with its model, task, and evaluation setup instead of comparing scores across conditions. Studies in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support share three requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and constraint-sensitive decisions. Stronger representations or higher benchmark scores can leave the claimed alignment mechanism unresolved, which motivates four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, targeted repair from failure diagnosis, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.

paper_title: A Survey of Security in Real-World Agents: From Digital Agents to Embodied AI
paper_abstract: Real-world agents extend language-model reasoning to digital operations and physical action, raising a central security question: how do digital-side attacks cross trust boundaries in robotic systems, and what physical safety conclusions can existing evidence support? This survey examines semantic hijacking, sensory manipulation, and middleware injection across software agents, modular robotic agents, and vision-language-action (VLA) systems. We compare how untrusted content acquires task authority, corrupted observations affect action generation, and middleware access reaches execution interfaces under different permission and control assumptions. An experiment-level analysis examines environment, trajectory, privilege and exposure, consequence, and assurance, distinguishing generated plans, software-state changes, simulated execution, and physical robot actions. The comparison reveals important evidence boundaries: RoboPAIR evaluates driving plans in Dolphins but API-mediated robot actions in Jackal, while Apollo point-cloud replay demonstrates altered braking decisions without measuring physical deceleration. These differences prevent planning or command-level success from being treated as direct evidence of physical safety violations. Across defenses, protection depends on the integrity of the state used for checking, coverage of executable command paths, and the timing of intervention. Reported attack suppression also need not imply useful protection: Safe Prompting reduces targeted attack success to zero while clean-task success also falls to zero in its LIBERO evaluation. Together, these findings identify the conditions under which digital compromise reaches physical execution, delimit the safety claims supported by current experiments, and motivate stronger assurance of action enforcement and recovery under compromised state.

paper_title: A Survey of Automatic Humor Detection: From Theoretical Foundations to Large Language Models
paper_abstract: Automatic humor detection, the computational task of identifying humorous content, is increasingly critical as Large Language Models (LLMs) integrate into communication platforms such as chatbots and virtual assistants. However, humor poses challenges for AI due to its reliance on context, cultural nuances, linguistic ambiguity, and multimodal cues. Current research is fragmented across humor types, languages, modalities, and evaluation benchmarks, particularly regarding modern LLM capabilities and limitations. This survey synthesizes the automatic humor detection field, tracing its evolution from foundational psychological and linguistic theories through classical machine learning, deep learning, and transformer-based LLMs. We organize and analyze computational methods, feature engineering techniques, benchmark datasets (text-only, multimodal, multilingual), and evaluation metrics. We examine LLM adaptation strategies, including fine-tuning, parameter-efficient methods (PEFT), prompt engineering, and multi-task learning, alongside multimodal and cross-lingual humor understanding developments. Our analysis reveals that while LLMs show improved performance in capturing surface humor patterns, gaps persist in pragmatic reasoning, cultural grounding, multimodal integration, and explainability. We identify open challenges, including data scarcity, evaluation inconsistencies, the humor–offensiveness boundary, and the need for culturally aware and interpretable models. By consolidating progress and pinpointing limitations, this survey guides future interdisciplinary research toward developing socially intelligent AI systems capable of understanding humor.

paper_title: Industry 4.0, Quality and Industry 4.0. Implementation in Slovakia: A Longitudinal Analysis Based on the Industry 4UM Survey (2017–2025)
paper_abstract: Industry 4.0 has become a key driver of industrial digital transformation, enabling enterprises to improve productivity, flexibility, and competitiveness through the integration of advanced digital technologies. Although the strategic importance of Industry 4.0 is widely recognized, the pace and maturity of its implementation vary considerably across enterprises and regions. This study presents a longitudinal evaluation of Industry 4.0 adoption in the Slovak Republic based on annual Industry4UM survey data collected between 2017 and 2025. The analysis focuses on three indicators: the size distribution of participating enterprises, the implementation phase of Industry 4.0, and the perceived importance of Industry 4.0 for future business development. The results indicate that the survey maintained participation from enterprises of different sizes throughout the observation period, providing a broad representation of the Slovak industrial environment. The implementation analysis revealed a gradual increase in the proportion of enterprises reaching the adaptation phase, accompanied by a substantial decline in the number of organizations that had not yet initiated Industry 4.0 activities. At the same time, respondents consistently expressed a highly positive perception of Industry 4.0, while negative attitudes remained negligible. A comparison of enterprise perception and implementation demonstrates that awareness of Industry 4.0 has advanced more rapidly than practical adoption, indicating that the principal challenge is no longer recognizing the importance of digital transformation but facilitating its effective implementation. The findings provide a comprehensive overview of the evolution of Industry 4.0 adoption in Slovak industry and offer insights that may support policymakers, researchers, and industrial practitioners in designing future digital transformation strategies. In this article, we also examine the State of Israel’s approach to Industry 4.0 from several perspectives. We focus on how both the Israeli industrial sector and government agencies support and implement Industry 4.0. Israeli government agencies, businesses, and institutions also focus on social and economic issues and on structural changes in the labour market related to Industry 4.0.

paper_title: Beyond the Symptom Score: What Standard Psychiatric Rating Scales Fail to Capture — A Narrative Review
paper_abstract: Standard psychiatric rating scales such as the PANSS, HAM-D and MADRS remain the dominant outcome measures in clinical trials and routine care, yet they were built to quantify symptom severity rather than to register the full range of change that matters to patients. This narrative review synthesized psychometric, validation, epidemiological and trial evidence, together with consensus reports, to identify clinically and personally meaningful improvements that symptom-focused scales fail to detect. Evidence converged on ten under-measured outcome domains: real-world functioning, which correlates only weakly with symptoms and often lags behind them; cognition and social cognition; negative symptoms and motivational anhedonia; the subjective experience of medication; quality of life and positive mental health; personal recovery (connectedness, hope, identity, meaning and empowerment); internalized stigma; physical health and premature mortality, with all-cause mortality two to three-and-a-half times that of the general population; sleep and circadian function; and shared decision-making as a process outcome of care. Two cross-cutting limitations compound these gaps: systematic discordance among clinician, self-report and informant ratings, and the inability of retrospective, clinic-based instruments to capture the momentary, context-dependent dynamics now accessible through ecological momentary assessment and passive sensing. We propose a pragmatic, tiered outcome set that pairs every symptom scale with measures of functioning and of quality of life or recovery, adds physical health, sleep and medication burden, and reserves digital methods for settings that can support them. Improvement in psychiatry is multidimensional; measuring it as such is a scientific necessity, not a refinement.

paper_title: Cancer Information Burden and Mental Health Among U.S. Cancer Caregivers: Evidence from the Health Information National Trends Survey
paper_abstract: Background: Family and unpaid caregivers play an essential role in supporting individuals with cancer and frequently navigate complex health information related to treatment, symptoms, supportive care, and healthcare services. Difficulty obtaining, understanding, and evaluating cancer information may contribute to psychological distress among caregivers. However, nationally representative evidence examining the association between cancer information burden and caregiver psychological well-being remains limited. Objective: This study examined the association between cancer information burden and psychological distress among U.S. adults who reported providing care to an individual with cancer. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of pooled data from the National Cancer Institute’s Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) Cycles 6 and 7. Cancer caregivers were identified based on respondents reporting caregiving for an individual with cancer. Cancer information burden was measured using four items assessing the effort required to obtain cancer information, difficulty understanding cancer information, frustration during cancer information seeking, and concern about information quality. Item responses were averaged to create a composite cancer information burden score, with higher scores indicating greater burden. Psychological distress was measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4), a validated 4-item measure of depressive and anxiety symptoms ranging from 0 to 12. Survey-weighted linear regression examined the association between cancer information burden and PHQ-4 scores while accounting for the complex survey design. Adjusted models included age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, and household income. Results: We identified 241 respondents as cancer caregivers, with 124 included in the fully adjusted complete-case analysis. In the common analytic sample, higher cancer information burden was associated with greater psychological distress in unadjusted analysis (β=1.57, 95% CI 0.17-2.98; p=.028). After adjustment for age, sex, race and ethnicity, education, and household income, the association remained statistically significant (β=0.89, 95% CI 0.03-1.75; p=.042). Older age was associated with lower psychological distress in the fully adjusted model (β=-0.06, 95% CI -0.11 to -0.01; p=.013). Several education and income categories were also associated with psychological distress. Diagnostic analyses supported an approximately linear relationship between information burden and PHQ-4 scores, although heteroskedasticity was present. Conclusions: Greater cancer information burden was associated with higher psychological distress among U.S. cancer caregivers. These findings suggest that caregiver well-being may be influenced not only by access to cancer information but also by the effort, complexity, frustration, and uncertainty involved in navigating that information. Interventions and digital health resources designed for cancer caregivers should therefore consider strategies to reduce information burden and improve caregivers' ability to identify, understand, and evaluate cancer-related information.

paper_title: Can Patients Be Highly Satisfied Despite Little Clinical Improvement—or Dissatisfied Despite Substantial Improvement? A Narrative Review
paper_abstract: Patient satisfaction has become a dominant metric of health care quality, embedded in public reporting, accreditation, and pay-for-performance programs. Its prominence rests on an implicit assumption that satisfied patients have been treated well and have improved. This narrative review synthesizes conceptual and empirical literature to examine whether, how often, and why patients can be highly satisfied despite minimal clinical gain or dissatisfied despite substantial gain. The 2 constructs are related but explain little of each other. In a cohort of 2116 surgical patients, no outcome measure accounted for more than 8% of the variance in satisfaction, which tracked absolute postoperative state rather than change. Complications and readmissions show weak, inconsistent associations with satisfaction, whereas communication and shared decision-making are strongly and independently associated with it. Six mechanisms explain the divergence: expectancy disconfirmation (unmet expectations raised the odds of dissatisfaction after knee arthroplasty more than 10-fold), relational determinants, health-status confounding, placebo and nocebo effects, response shift (detected in 86.7% of longitudinal studies), and measurement artifacts such as ceiling effects and response bias. In low- and middle-income settings, more than half of respondents rated poor-quality care as good or better. Satisfaction should be neither discarded nor used as a surrogate for effectiveness; complementary measurement of care experience, clinical outcome, and expectation fulfillment is the defensible path.

paper_title: Artificial Intelligence and Engagement Pricing in Accounting Firms: A Literature Review and Research Agenda
paper_abstract: Accounting firms are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) quickly, but the way they plan and price engagements has changed much more slowly. This paper reviews research from four areas that rarely meet: the pricing of accounting and audit services, the productivity effects of AI on knowledge work, the use of AI in accounting and auditing, and activity-based costing and project control. The review finds that AI's effects on accounting work are large but uneven across tasks, that new review and oversight work appears alongside time savings, and that hours freed by AI are often absorbed by other work rather than appearing as lower recorded effort. Firm-level studies link AI investment to lower audit fees and to changes in staff mix, but almost no research examines how firms adjust the internal, hours-based plans on which fees are set. I identify six gaps: the measurement of activity-level AI effects, the cost of oversight, the fate of freed capacity, in-engagement monitoring, the sharing of AI gains with clients, and the position of small and mid-sized practices. I then propose a research agenda of seven questions with suggested methods and data. The paper aims to help researchers and practitioners study and manage AI-enabled engagements on the basis of evidence rather than general efficiency assumptions.

paper_title: Responsible and Trustworthy Agentic AI: Governance, Assurance, Explainability, Controllability, and Human Oversight: A Comprehensive Survey
paper_abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence combines goal-directed reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, adaptation and multi-agent coordination with the ability to affect external systems. This capability raises problems of authorization, safety, human oversight, accountability and the evidence required to justify reliance. This non-systematic integrative survey distinguishes AI ethics, responsible AI, governance, trustworthiness, assurance, explainability, security and controllability; synthesizes preventive, detective, corrective, human-based and agent-based controls; and compares responsibility and oversight arrangements across the agent lifecycle. Building on established governance and meaningful-human-control research, it proposes an authority-control-assurance-accountability mapping that connects normative requirements to delegated decision rights, enforceable controls, observable evidence, escalation conditions and identifiable organizational owners. Two fictional cases illustrate the proposed mapping for document access and software changes. The framework is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirically validated assurance standard. The survey identifies limitations of supervisory-agent independence, long-horizon explanation, dynamic authorization and continuous re-assurance, and specifies research questions for future evaluation.

paper_title: Academic Integrity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Scoping Review (2026)
paper_abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed the landscape of modern higher education, prompting a critical paradigm shift in how academic integrity is conceptualized. This scoping review synthesizes 20 cutting-edge academic publications from 2026 (retrieved via Google Scholar) to examine the evolution of academic integrity from mechanical plagiarism detection and punitive surveillance toward comprehensive institutional, pedagogical, and ethical redesign. The synthesis reveals that the primary systemic catalyst for academic misconduct remains the pervasive “publish or perish” culture and quantitative assessment paradigms that prioritize performance over moral growth. Contemporary scholarship moves beyond identifying individual infractions to address systemic vulnerabilities, student uncertainty, data privacy, and the degradation of higher-order cognitive skills (analyzing, evaluating, creating) resulting from unreflective AI reliance. To mitigate these threats, the review highlights four key integrative strategies: (1) adoption of ecosystemic models (e.g., A. Maleki’s Higher Education Integrity Ecosystem) linking governance, assessment, cultural norms, and individual agency; (2) implementation of process-oriented, authentic assessment frameworks (e.g., S. Lehane, A. Wright and P. Fenton’s Model for Practice and P.D.N. Ncube et al.’s PRISMA-based multi-stage evaluations) that render automated cheating obsolete; (3) operationalization of the AI3 model that integrated AI, academic integrity, and assessment innovation (C. DeLuca, L.Volante and M. Holden), and (4) proactive educational initiatives, AI literacy, and epistemic pluralism to safeguard neurodivergent learning trajectories. Ultimately, the academic community is transitioning from technocratic panic to building ethically resilient, adaptive educational ecosystems aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 4 and SDG 16).

paper_title: Barriers and Facilitators to the Implementation of Pre-Symptomatic Genetic Testing in Clinical Practice: An Updated Systematic Review
paper_abstract: Pre-symptomatic genetic and genomic testing can identify individuals at increased disease risk before symptoms emerge, but implementation depends on patient, clinician, organisational and system factors. This updated systematic review examined barriers and facilitators to implementation after the search period of Shen et al. (through 22 May 2020). PubMed was searched on 3 August 2026 using three independently constructed search sets for genetic/genomic testing, presymptomatic/asymptomatic screening, and implementation-related evidence, combined as #1 AND #2 AND #3. English-language records from 2020–2026 were screened, with publication dates audited against the update boundary. One reviewer conducted screening, eligibility assessment, design-appropriate JBI critical appraisal, extraction and narrative thematic synthesis. Of 824 records identified before filtering, 347 were screened, 91 reports were sought, 80 full texts were assessed, and 63 studies were included. Across 424 extracted barrier/facilitator findings, system-level determinants were most frequent (141 findings across 47 studies), followed by patient-level determinants (103 across 40). Thirty-four of 58 themes from Shen et al. were confirmed, while 17 additional themes were identified, including care-pathway design and follow-up, health equity and representativeness, workforce capacity, organisational readiness, logistics, and family dynamics. The post-2020 evidence places greater emphasis on operational delivery and health-system capacity, although comparisons with the earlier review are limited by PubMed-only coverage and a single-reviewer workflow. Implementation should therefore be understood as a care pathway extending beyond the genetic test itself.

paper_title: Designing Digital Courses for 21st-Century and Future Skills in Open Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
paper_abstract: Background: Higher education increasingly uses digital, blended, flipped, and open online learning to develop 21st-century skills. However, evidence on their effectiveness remains fragmented across disciplines and learning contexts. Objective: To synthesize evidence on the effects of digitally redesigned courses on 21st-century and future-oriented skills among higher- and professional-education learners.Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA 2020. Comparative quantitative studies evaluating digital, blended, flipped, or open online course designs against traditional or alternative instruction were eligible. A second search covered studies published from 2024–2026. Study quality was assessed using an MMAT-informed approach. Random-effects meta-analyses using restricted maximum likelihood estimation were conducted in STATA 17, with Hedges’ g and 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed using I², τ², Q, and H², and publication bias using contour-enhanced funnel plots and Egger’s test. Results: Nineteen studies were included. Digital course designs showed a moderate-to-large positive effect on 21st-century skills (Hedges’ g = 0.73, 95% CI 0.68–0.78; p < 0.001), with moderate heterogeneity (τ² = 0.01; I² = 46.54%). Effects differed significantly by pedagogical approach, OER use, assessment type, and frequency of use. The largest effects were observed for constructivist-CBE hybrid approaches (g = 0.87), portfolio-based assessment (g = 0.94), and continuous use (g = 0.83). No significant differences were found by delivery format or geographic region. Funnel-plot findings suggested possible publication bias. Conclusions: Digitally redesigned courses can strengthen 21st-century skills, particularly when technology supports active, task-oriented learning and continuous assessment. More skill-specific studies outside health-professions education are needed.

paper_title: Assessment in the Age of Generative AI: Academic Integrity, Authentic Learning and Assessment Design in Tanzanian Universities — A Systematic Review
paper_abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT can now produce essays, problem solutions and examination answers that pass as competent student work, raising the question of whether university grades still show what students know and can do. This systematic review with thematic synthesis examined what the international and African literature reports on GenAI and academic integrity, the effectiveness and fairness of AI detection, and the assessment designs that hold up in an AI-rich environment. Following PRISMA 2020, seven databases and organisational sources were searched for studies published between January 2018 and June 2026. Thirty studies were included, eleven from Africa and four from Tanzania; they were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, AMSTAR 2 and the AACODS checklist and synthesised thematically with frequency counts. Five themes emerged: widespread and rising student use of GenAI (50% of studies); the vulnerability of conventional take-home and online assessment (60%); the unreliability and unfairness of AI-detection software (27%); the partial protection offered by authentic, process-focused and oral assessment (37%); and policy, capacity and training gaps (60%), most acute in African institutions. The evidence indicates that Tanzanian universities cannot rely on detection. They should move from a policing model to a design model of integrity, supported by institutional guidance, staff development and a graded scale of acceptable AI use. A Tanzanian Assessment Redesign Framework (TARF) is proposed for empirical testing, and priorities for intervention research are identified.

paper_title: From Aligned Embeddings to Instruction-Following Perception: A Survey of Vision–Language Model Development
paper_abstract: Recognizing an object from a text label, describing an unfamiliar scene, and following an instruction about a small image region require different forms of visual-language correspondence. The development of vision-language models can be understood through the effort to support these increasingly varied outputs. This survey follows the transition from contrastive image-text representations to captioning and grounding systems, and then to instruction-tuned multimodal language models. Within this account, we examine how pretraining objectives, web-data curation, visual connectors, and adaptation methods affect the tasks a model can perform. Particular attention is given to novel object captioning and dense prediction: both expose information that can be lost when image-level alignment is used as the starting point for a more specific task. Relative contrastive alignment [Fan et al., 2023] and uncertainty-guided cross-head co-training [Fan et al., 2022] offer complementary case studies of supervision quality. Evaluation and hallucination are considered alongside the capabilities they are meant to measure. The review brings together architectural comparisons, task-oriented evidence, and unresolved questions about visual resolution, grounding, and benchmark validity. Its central concern is how a system’s training signal and representation support the visual claims it ultimately makes.

paper_title: From Human Corrections to Learned Segmentations: A Critical Mathematical Review of Information, Learning, and Human Effort
paper_abstract: When does a human correction become useful learning, and what establishes better segmentation at matched human effort? This critical narrative review follows feedback through its selection, learner update, and evaluation. It compares active learning, machine teaching, interactive segmentation, and sequential predictive evaluation using a common mathematical account of target information, predictive error, response predictability, and human work. An exact Bayesian update converts evaluation-label information into expected log-loss improvement; an excess-risk decomposition explains what an approximate learner can lose. Conditional information decompositions separate the roles of selected locations, labels, and displayed context. Empirical comparisons show why response protocols, update mechanisms, and effort denominators matter, distinguishing current-mask refinement from reusable learning and simulated interaction from human evidence. We identify what logs can reveal, what requires independent evaluation, and what remains model-dependent. The resulting research priorities are to test what selection reveals, whether using it improves assimilation, and whether the resulting interaction policy benefits segmentation at matched effort. These are distinct claims: predicting a teacher's responses need not identify human intentions or establish better learning. No new acquisition algorithm or empirical superiority is claimed.
comments: 40 pages, literature-selection and search record included

paper_title: Can We Believe AI Peer Review?
paper_abstract: As large language models become widely used in scientific review and manuscript revision, AI scores are increasingly serving as feedback for assessing paper quality and guiding edits. Yet whether a single AI score reliably reflects the reviewer's judgment, and whether revision gains based on that score are endorsed by other reviewers, remain understudied. Using 200 papers from ICLR 2025 and 2026 and approximately 14,000 AI reviews, we study score reliability, score-distribution estimation, and cross-model agreement on revision gains. Repeated reviews fluctuate even under identical conditions. Finer-grained scoring protocols reduce score variance but also systematically shift mean scores, while the gains assigned to manuscript revisions depend strongly on the reviewer.

paper_title: Towards Adaptive and Real-Survey-Aligned Simulated Urban Mobility Behaviour of Generative Agents
paper_abstract: In existing agent-based simulations of multimodal urban mobility, agents, representing humans, choose their travel modes either using discrete choice or machine learning models fitted on structured travel survey data, or with rules explicitly written by the domain experts. Such approaches fix a priori the agents' possible behaviour space. Hence, a factor absent from variables or rules cannot affect agents' decisions. In reality, choosing a transport mode is a multidimensional decision in which objective and subjective factors intertwine and change over time. Integrating such complexity into a city-scale multimodal mobility simulation remains a challenge. Generative agents (GAs) built on large language models promise to respond to this challenge because they carry decision heuristics that travel surveys do not record. However, to the best of our knowledge, aligning their decisions with real household travel surveys remains an open question. In this paper, we build an agent-based model of daily multimodal mobility for Toulouse (France). We compare the performance of fifteen decision-makers (simple baselines, models fitted on the survey, GAs with minimal and tuned prompts, and a typed classifier) on the real household travel survey. Our results show that GAs with tuned prompts come close to the fitted models on the modal split of a simulated day without transport disruptions, but not trip by trip. GAs also react when unforeseen events occur. The recently released Jev-1.13 TypeSafe classifier gives surprisingly great results, showing that generating output text is not necessary. The results presented in this paper would be of interest to transport policy makers and service providers looking to apply generative agent-based modelling for improving urban mobility services.

paper_title: Learning Checklists to Reduce Lottery Effects in Scientific Peer Review
paper_abstract: Reviewer lottery error describes error due to a small set of peer reviews attending to only some of the issues with a paper that a larger pool of eligible reviewers would raise. We show this error can be reduced by surfacing a checklist of criticisms learned from a historical review corpus. Our approach generates a tree of checklists representing coarsenings of the atomic review claim space, then selects the coarsening that maximizes a theoretically-motivated measure of correlated agreement among reviewers. We realize this approach with an LLM-assisted pipeline and test it on NeurIPS 2021 and ICLR 2022 review data. In simulated review with LLM reviewers, the learned checklist reduces the mean squared error (MSE) of a three reviewer committee by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR, and on both venues the checklist with the highest correlated agreement has the lowest error for committees of three or more. In a human study with 20 participants, the learned NeurIPS checklist lowers the MSE of a paper ranking, measured against the NeurIPS 2021 order, from 0.48 to 0.22.

paper_title: Multiheme Cytochrome c7 Expansion Is a Phylum-Level Trait of the Candidate Phylum Kryptonia: A Survey of 22,307 Prokaryotic Genomes
paper_abstract: Background: Multiheme c-type cytochromes (MHCs) are the principal conduits of extracellular electron transfer (EET) in dissimilatory metal-reducing bacteria, yet their distribution across recently described candidate phyla remains poorly resolved. The cytochrome c7 family (triheme per core module) is a widespread MHC lineage whose phylum-level copy-number architecture has never been systematically surveyed. Methods: We scanned 22,307 prokaryotic genomes spanning candidate and established phyla with a dedicated c7-family profile HMM (E < 0.01), quantified per-genome copy numbers and CXXCH heme-binding motif loads, and benchmarked Kryptonia against Aquificota, DPANN, CPR, and a broad genomic background. Results: All 51 Kryptonia genomes encode c7 homologs, with a median of 15 copies per genome (max 19; 100% of genomes ≥5 copies; 88% ≥10) — the highest median per-genome dosage of any surveyed clade. By contrast, the largest Aquificota family (Aquificaceae) encodes a median of 1 copy, DPANN a median of 0 (max 6), and 98.9% of 20,217 background genomes carry fewer than 5. Kryptonia c7 proteins are also enriched in large MHCs: 49% carry ≥9 CXXCH motifs, versus 15–25% in CPR/DPANN. Canonical and divergent (novel) copies co-occur in 49/51 genomes, indicating a mixed repertoire rather than fixation of a single variant. Conclusions: High-copy, mixed-composition c7 repertoires are a phylum-level trait of Kryptonia rather than an isolate-specific anomaly, positioning this candidate phylum as a previously unrecognized reservoir of multiheme electron-transfer architecture.

paper_title: A Comprehensive Survey on LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search
paper_abstract: Large Language Model-guided Evolutionary Search (LLM-ES), exemplified by AlphaEvolve, has recently demonstrated impressive performance in solving goal-driven problems with extremely large and complex search spaces. Unlike conventional LLM approaches based on single-shot or few-shot sampling, LLM-ES introduces population-based evolution to iteratively generate more novel and higher-quality solutions. Compared with traditional Evolutionary Computing algorithms, LLM-ES treats LLMs as semantic variation operators. This design extends the search space from low-dimensional vectors to expressive and language-defined structures such as code and programs. Meanwhile, the rich prior knowledge embedded in LLMs significantly improves the efficiency of evolutionary search in complex solution spaces. As a result, LLM-ES effectively exploits the test-time scaling capability of LLMs and achieves state-of-the-art performance in many open-ended problems. In this survey, we provide a systematic overview of this emerging field. We first formalize the problem setting and the general pipeline of LLM-ES. We then review existing works from several key perspectives, including population design, prompt builder, LLM model selection, evaluation design, and exploration-exploitation control. Finally, we summarize representative applications and discuss open challenges and future research directions.

paper_title: Applications of Quartz Sand in Petroleum Production and Engineering Material Selection: A Comprehensive Review
paper_abstract: Quartz sand is used throughout oil and gas well engineering, including hydraulic fracturing, wellbore sand control, high-temperature cementing and produced-water treatment, but each use imposes distinct require-ments on particle size, morphology, strength, reactivity and cleanliness. Following the performance chain from mineral source, washing and size classification, storage and transport, slurry injection and fracture placement to long-term service, this review discusses proppant transport and settling, bridging and bed-load migration, breakage and wall embedment under closure stress, fines migration, fracture-fluid residues, mul-tiphase and non-Darcy flow, stress cycling and time-dependent damage. Natural quartz sand, pre-cured and curable resin-coated sands, ceramic proppants and mixed proppants are compared. Material selection should be based on target-well long-term conductivity tests and life-cycle economics. The review also considers gravel packing, where grain-size matching to formation sand, screen compatibility and packing completeness are critical, and high-temperature well cementing, where finely ground silica regulates the calcium-to-silicon ra-tio of hydration products and mitigates strength retrogression. API Std 19C and ISO 13503-2:2024 provide the basic characterization framework, whereas ISO 13503-5:2006 can organize long-term conductivity compari-son but does not provide an absolute in-situ conductivity. A project-level test matrix, minimum reporting set and batch-traceability loop are proposed for resource assessment, product development, procurement and field verification.

paper_title: Biomedical Applications of Nanotechnology in Chronic Kidney Disease: A Thematic and Translational Review with Supporting Bibliometric Analysis
paper_abstract: Background: Nanotechnology has expanded biomedical applications in chronic kidney disease (CKD), including diagnostics, monitoring, targeted therapy, and extracorporeal management. However, heterogeneity in materials, experimental models, and translational development complicates assessment of clinical progress. This review characterized major CKD nanotechnology applications and their documented translational stages, supported by complementary bibliometric analysis. Methods: English-language original studies indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE between July 1, 2021, and July 1, 2026, were organized into 11 overlapping thematic categories and classified according to their highest documented translational stage. Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny characterized publication, journal, institutional, and geographic patterns, while VOSviewer analyzed MeSH term co-occurrence. Results: Of 288 records identified, 160 studies across 91 journals were included. The most frequent categories were nanodiagnostics and biosensors (53 studies), nanotherapy for renal fibrosis (51), kidney-targeted drug delivery (28), and redox nanomedicine, inflammation, and oxidative stress (27). Diagnostic platforms more frequently reached human-sample validation or early clinical evaluation, whereas therapeutic approaches remained predominantly preclinical. Extracorporeal nanotechnologies were largely experimental, with limited human-sample evaluation. The 10 most productive journals accounted for 55 studies (34.4%), illustrating the concentration of publications within a multidisciplinary field. Conclusions: CKD nanomedicine exhibits substantial technological diversity but uneven translational development. Progress toward clinical implementation requires standardized physicochemical characterization, reproducibility, independent validation, long-term safety assessment, manufacturing scalability, and rigorous comparisons with established standards of care using clinically meaningful outcomes.

paper_title: A Systematic Review of Impacts of Land Policies on Historically Disadvantaged Individuals in South Africa
paper_abstract: Introduction: Land policies are frequently presented as instruments for correcting colonial, racial, feudal and elite‐concentrated land inequality. Across the supplied literature, however, formal redistribution, restitution, recognition and titling do not consistently produce secure tenure or improved socioeconomic conditions for historically disadvantaged populations. This systematic review examined how land reform, redistribution, restitution, tenure regularization and titling relate to socioeconomic impacts and tenure security, while identifying enabling conditions, risks and implementation barriers. Methods: The researcher‐selected databases and information sources were Google Scholar, PubMed (MEDLINE) and ERIC. The eligibility protocol restricted publication years to 2025–2026. The exact calendar date of search execution was not recorded in the verified identification provenance; this is distinct from the publication‐year eligibility range. Google Scholar, PubMed (MEDLINE) and ERIC were searched using the supplied Boolean strategy for English peer‐ reviewed studies published between 2025 and 2026. Results: Land reform was consistently framed as a project of distributive and reparative justice, but redistribution was constrained by political instability, elite accommodation, weak administrative capacity, regulatory overlap and inadequate conflict resolution. Formal recognition frequently protected only partial or selected rights. Socioeconomic benefits depended on complementary water, infrastructure, inputs, services, livelihood support and recognition of local knowledge. Poorly planned reform, conservation restrictions and resettlement generated displacement, livelihood disruption, food insecurity and conflict. Participation, inclusion, accessible information, accountability and free, prior and informed consent were recurrent enabling conditions. Discussion/Conclusion: Land policies can advance justice and livelihood security, but their effects are conditional rather than automatic. Effective reform requires institutional capacity, substantive redistribution, inclusive tenure recognition and integrated socioeconomic support.

paper_title: Effects of Endosymbionts on Arthropod Behavior: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
paper_abstract: Facultative endosymbionts living within arthropod cells are known to affect several aspects their hosts’ behavior. Here we synthesize studies that measure effects of endosymbionts on arthropod behavioral traits, ranging from effects on host activity and feeding to mating and multitrophic interactions with predators and parasitoids. Our systematic review of the literature identified 70 laboratory studies that compared behavioral traits between arthropod populations where the endosymbiont was either present or absent. In a meta-analysis of 799 comparisons (639 Hedges’ g effect sizes and 160 log of odds ratios for binomial data) across different endosymbiont species and behavioral categories, we found that the presence of facultative endosymbionts tended to provide benefits to mating but costs to feeding, while for many other traits endosymbionts had no overall effect or patterns depended on the endosymbiont or host species. Measured effects of endosymbionts tended to be larger when the genetic background of the strains was not controlled. We discuss challenges with assessing effects of endosymbionts on arthropod behavior, identify avenues for future studies and highlight implications for field releases of arthropod lines carrying endosymbionts for pest and pathogen control.

paper_title: Trustworthy Federated Intrusion Detection for the Future Internet: A Critical Review and Evaluation Framework
paper_abstract: Federated intrusion detection for the Future Internet must operate across heterogeneous devices, distributed telemetry, changing traffic patterns, and adversarial clients. This critical structured review synthesizes a targeted corpus of 37 publications and standards, including 20 Future Internet articles, coded on six methodological evidence dimensions using a transparent ordinal rubric. Federated-learning relevance received the highest mean coverage score (3.32/5; 24 of 37 records scored at least 3), followed by reproducibility (2.89/5; 19 of 37). Evidence for robustness (1.19/5; 10 of 37), generalization (1.00/5; 7 of 37), explainability (1.27/5; 7 of 37), and deployment realism (1.59/5; 10 of 37) was markedly sparser. Only five records scored at least 3 on both robustness and generalization. These results describe the methods addressed in a purposefully selected literature corpus, not the performance of deployed detection systems. Based on the observed coverage gaps, we propose a reproducible evaluation framework encompassing non-independent and identically distributed federation, disjoint and open-set testing, poisoning and backdoor attacks, leakage auditing, explanation stability, and edge-resource measurements. A supplementary Excel workbook separates original source-level coding from formula-linked analyses and sensitivity checks. Trustworthy federated intrusion detection should be evaluated through this joint systems-level evidence rather than closed-world predictive accuracy alone.

paper_title: Social Relationships in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Profound Shifts and New Challenges—An Integrative Literature Review
paper_abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from a tool for information retrieval to a partner in conversation, advice, and emotional support. This integrative review examines whether that shift is reshaping friendship and other social bonds. Drawing on relationship science, human–machine communication research, surveys, experiments, longitudinal panels, randomized trials, and meta-analyses published through September 2026, including emerging evidence from Arab societies, the review develops the Responsiveness–Reciprocity Bridge Model to explain why conversational AI can relieve loneliness in the moment yet fail to build the relational capital that sustains people over time. A substantial minority of adolescents and young adults already turn to chatbots when they feel sad, anxious, or lonely, and short-term interactions with companion systems can reduce loneliness about as much as talking with another person, largely because users feel heard. These gains do not establish that synthetic ties can replace human friendship. Close relationships require mutual need, sacrifice, shared history, and practical solidarity that chatbots do not provide; in a randomized experiment, a human peer outperformed a highly supportive chatbot, and longitudinal and large-sample studies associate intensive, companionship-oriented use with greater loneliness and lower well-being. In Arab contexts, culturally aligned and human-guided digital tools show promise, but claims that AI is widely replacing traditional friends are not supported by comparable prevalence research. The central implication is balance: AI can widen access to support, but only if it is designed, governed, and used as a bridge to human relationships rather than as a substitute for them.

paper_title: Family Socioeconomic Status and Child and Adolescent Developmental Outcomes: A Review and Meta-Analysis
paper_abstract: Lower family socioeconomic status (SES) is widely linked to poorer child development, but the magnitude of the association varies across outcomes and samples. To synthesise correlational evidence on SES and externalizing/antisocial behaviour, internalizing/depressive symptoms, and language/literacy in children and adolescents. Multiple databases including Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed/MEDLINE were searched. Reports were screened against a pre-specified protocol (age ≤ 10 years; income/SES exposure; positive developmental outcomes), and effects were extracted as SES–outcome correlations (Fisher z). A post-hoc synthesis of the reported outcomes was undertaken with random-effects models, subgroup analysis by outcome domain, meta-regression, sensitivity analysis and funnel-plot/Egger tests using Stata version 17. 12 studies were included. Eight studies examined relations with externalizing outcomes (r = 0.04, 95% CI: 0.11, 0.03), and 6 studies examined relations with internalizing outcomes (r = 0.04, 95% CI: 0.12, 0.05). Language/literacy outcomes showed positive relations to SES (r = 0.24-0.46; exploratory pooled r = 0.38, 95% CI: 0.26, 0.49), with outcome domain accounting for significant between-subgroup heterogeneity. Mainly adolescents, family SES was weakly and inconsistently related to externalising and internalising problems, and prediction intervals were large. Language/literacy had a more robust positive SES gradient but only two small independent samples.

paper_title: The Spectrum of Penetrating Craniocerebral Injuries in Pakistan: A Narrative Review
paper_abstract: Background: Although penetrating craniocerebral injuries (PCIs) are rare, they can be extremely serious and are linked with a high level of neurological morbidity and mortality. In Pakistan, published work mainly consists of individual case reports and small case series, with wide variation in mechanisms, anatomical paths, radiological findings, surgical methods, and outcomes. This narrative review aims to bring together the existing literature on various types of penetrating brain and craniocerebral injuries in Pakistan and describe their clinical, radiological, and management characteristics. Methods: Studies were screened against predefined eligibility criteria, with an emphasis on injuries caused by penetrating objects, including unusual low-velocity foreign bodies. Relevant information was extracted on the mechanism and circumstances of injury; clinical and neurological presentation; anatomical entry site and trajectory; depth and location of the foreign body; radiological characteristics; surgical management; and postoperative outcomes and complications. Results: Six Pakistani publications met the eligibility criteria and were included in the narrative synthesis. The reported injuries demonstrated considerable heterogeneity in the type of penetrating object, anatomical entry site, trajectory, and intracranial location. Penetration occurred through different cranial and facial regions, with foreign bodies traversing cortical and deeper intracranial structures in some cases. Clinical presentation ranged from relatively preserved neurological status to severe neurological impairment, depending on the trajectory and structures involved. Computed tomography was central to defining the entry site, trajectory, depth, retained foreign body, and associated intracranial injuries. Despite the severity of some injuries, selected patients had favorable neurological outcomes, while complications included infection, neurological deficits, and other procedure- or injury-related sequelae. Conclusion: Pakistani literature demonstrates that PCIs are clinically diverse and require individualized assessment based on the entry site, trajectory, depth, and anatomical relationship of the foreign body to critical intracranial structures. However, evidence remains limited to a small number of case-based publications, highlighting the need for systematic reporting and larger multicenter studies to define better injury patterns, management strategies, complications, and long-term outcomes of PCIs in Pakistan.

paper_title: Error Enhancement in Physical Rehabilitation: From Motor Learning Theory to Robotic Neurorehabilitation– A Comprehensive Review
paper_abstract: Error enhancement (EE), also referred to as error augmentation (EA), represents a distinctive ap-proach to motor rehabilitation in which errors are not minimized but deliberately magnified in a controlled manner. The underlying premise is derived from contemporary theories of motor learning and sensorimotor adaptation: when the nervous system detects a discrepancy between the intended and actual consequences of a movement, this error provides a powerful teaching signal that can modify subsequent motor commands. Robotic systems make it possible to manipulate this error precisely by applying externally generated forces that deviate the limb from its intended trajectory. This review examines the theoretical basis of error enhancement, its development as a rehabilitation strategy in particular attention is given to studies conducted in healthy individuals and stroke survivors. The available evidence is then considered in relation to sensorimotor inte-gration, virtual reality, constraint-induced movement therapy, and the Bobath concept. Finally, the emergence of the BioXtreme/deXtreme robotic platform is discussed as a translational development that combines robotic force-field manipulation, three-dimensional movement, virtual reality and adaptive error enhancement. Although the evidence remains preliminary and larger controlled trials are required, error enhancement provides a compelling framework for converting movement error from a problem to be suppressed into a signal that can actively drive motor adaptation and rehabilitation.

paper_title: Long Non-Coding RNAs in Immune Thrombocytopenia: A Narrative Review of Pathogenesis and Clinical Implications
paper_abstract: Background/Objectives: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disease characterized by increased platelet destruction and insufficient platelet production. Accurate diagnosis, prognostic assessment, and treatment selection remain challenging. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) regulate immune responses and may contribute to ITP pathogenesis. This review examines lncRNA expression in ITP and its potential diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic relevance. Methods: We reviewed English-language literature published between 1994 and 2026 using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. We examined studies of specific lncRNAs in ITP, focusing on their expression differences and potential diagnostic and therapeutic implications. Re-sults: The studies examined HCP5, NEAT1, lnc-DC, IFNG-AS1, MEG3, GAS5, MALAT1, and THRIL. Findings suggest these lncRNAs may contribute to ITP pathogenesis and serve as candidate diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers. Some were reported as independent predictors of poor prognosis or were associated with glucocorticoid responsiveness. Potential applications include distinguishing primary from secondary ITP, informing patient selection for splenectomy, and identifying therapeutic targets. These applications remain investigational. Conclusions: Research on lncRNAs provides insight into autoimmune mechanisms underlying ITP and may support improvements in diagnosis, prognostic assessment, and individualized treatment. Although several lncRNAs show promise as biomarkers and therapeutic targets, further research, clinical validation, and methodological standardization are needed before routine clinical implementation.

paper_title: A Systematic Review of Crash Causes and Safety Trends in Automated Driving Systems and Advanced Driver Assistance Systems
paper_abstract: As Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) and Automated Driving Systems (ADS) technologies become more prevalent, evaluating their safety performance in complex, real-world environments has emerged as a critical research priority. This study presents a systematic literature review of crashes involving vehicles equipped with ADAS and ADS. Using the PRISMA methodology, this review analyzed 51 peer-reviewed articles and books published between 2018 and 2025. Articles were identified through comprehensive searches of ScienceDirect, TRID, and the Transportation Research Record. The selected studies were organized into five thematic categories: safety and crash characteristics, human interaction and user behavior, testing tools and simulations, cybersecurity and perception risks, and policy and governance. Findings reveal that while AV technologies show promise in reducing crash severity and frequency, performance is highly context-dependent, affected by roadway geometry, weather, system limitations, and user behavior. ADAS-related crashes are more common on highways and often involve human error, whereas ADS crashes are more likely in urban settings and linked to system disengagements. The review also highlights significant gaps in data availability, standardized evaluation protocols, and human-machine interaction research. Despite growing literature, many studies rely heavily on simulations and legacy datasets, limiting generalizability. To support safer AV deployment, future research must prioritize real-world testing and user trust frameworks deployment strategies. This review offers a knowledge base to guide policymakers, researchers, and industry stakeholders in advancing the development and regulation of vehicle automation technologies.

paper_title: Does Sexual Trauma Accelerate Biological Aging? A Narrative Review of Epigenetic, Cellular, Endocrine, Inflammatory and Metabolic Pathways
paper_abstract: Survivors of sexual violence carry a disproportionate burden of age-related morbidity, including cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and inflammatory conditions, raising the possibility that sexual trauma accelerates the biology of aging rather than acting solely through psychological distress or health behaviors. This narrative review synthesizes translational, epidemiological and biomarker evidence across five mechanistic domains. Epigenetically, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is associated with accelerated DNA-methylation age, most consistently on the mortality-calibrated GrimAge clock, whereas meta-analytic evidence for cumulative childhood adversity on first- and second-generation clocks is weak. At the cellular level, severe childhood sexual abuse is associated with shorter leukocyte telomeres in several, though not all, studies, and PTSD with telomere attrition, T-cell senescence and oxidative DNA damage. Endocrinologically, childhood sexual abuse produces enduring hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis sensitization and earlier pubertal maturation in girls. Inflammatory evidence is the most robust: childhood maltreatment prospectively predicts adult C-reactive protein, and PTSD is consistently associated with elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines. Metabolically, PTSD is associated with a high prevalence of metabolic syndrome, and childhood sexual abuse with obesity and type 2 diabetes in women. Glucocorticoid-FKBP5-NF-κB signaling and allostatic load emerge as bridges between domains, and we propose an integrated six-step model. Causal inference remains limited by retrospective trauma assessment, confounding by co-occurring adversity and scarce trauma-type-specific analyses. Priorities include prospective, sexual-trauma-specific multi-omic studies and trials testing whether trauma-focused, anti-inflammatory or metabolic interventions can slow the pace of biological aging in survivors.

paper_title: How Well Do LLMs Perform in Peer Review? Evidence from Finance and Accounting
paper_abstract: Referees increasingly use large language models (LLMs), while finance and accounting journals disagree about whether to allow it. We ask which part of a referee's job the models can do. GPT-4o, whose training data end before the 2024 conference season, referees the papers presented at the 2024 AFA and NBER finance meetings, and we compare its verdicts with publication in the top-three finance journals over the next two years. Papers the model scores one standard deviation higher are 44\% more likely to be published, net of author reputation. The result is not driven by look-ahead bias, as the model does not recall the outcomes. The information comes from its judgements of correctness and exposition. Its judgements of originality and significance carry none, and a referee guide that stresses importance does not help. The split between correctness and contribution holds for accounting papers and for a newer model, GPT-5. LLMs can check whether research is right, but not whether it matters. The technical check can go to the model, while the judgement of contribution stays with people.

paper_title: One-Sided Verification Under Limited Expert Review
paper_abstract: AI has become increasingly helpful in scientific discovery, yet human expert review remains essential for those problems without reliable automated evaluation, posing a fundamental challenge as candidate generation scales beyond available review capacity. This paper studies verification under limited human effort, where rare valid solutions need to be prioritized while invalid candidates should be filtered out to reduce human workload. We adopt the one-sided verification objective that maximizes the rejection rate of invalid solutions (TNR) under a constraint on the false-rejection rate of valid ones (FNR), making human review cost an explicit term to minimize. Drawing on the intuition that verifying a specific error can be easier than discovering one, we introduce OSVerify, an algorithmic framework that decouples error proposal from error validation. The error proposer searches for errors in solutions across different granularities by hierarchical decomposition, while the validator distinguishes substantial errors from minor or hallucinated ones. Experiments on competition- and research-level benchmarks show that OSVerify reduces the number of human reviews of invalid solutions by 46% on average compared to voting baselines under the same empirical low FNR constraint. Our post-training of the validator further improves the reduction to 57%. As high-impact real-world use cases, we apply OSVerify to identify errors in published research papers that are subsequently confirmed by the original authors and help resolve three Langlands open conjectures that are confirmed by experts, demonstrating its utility to facilitate human-AI research collaboration.

paper_title: Evaluating Security Claims in LLM Systems: A Survey of Adversarial Attacks and Defenses
paper_abstract: Attack success rates alone do not establish the security of large language model (LLM) systems because results depend on the attacker, deployment conditions, and measured consequence. This survey complements existing attack and defense taxonomies by examining what individual experiments actually support. We pair a threat model describing attacker capabilities and objectives with a defense model specifying observable information, security functions, and enforceable responses. An attack-defense assurance matrix determines whether an evaluation addresses the conditions relevant to a stated security claim. A bounded claim grammar also records the attacker, system version, consequence, cost, evaluation oracle, and other conditions that limit the result. An evidence ladder organizes empirical requirements for a fixed security claim and threat model without ranking papers or defenses. We apply the framework across model behavior, retrieval and memory, agents and tools, supply chains, privacy, availability, and serving infrastructure. The resulting synthesis helps researchers and practitioners distinguish demonstrated protection from untested conditions, compare results under matched assumptions, and design evaluations that measure the security consequences relevant to deployment.

paper_title: Summer Compound Hot-Drought Extreme Events over Northwest China: A Review of Recent Studies
paper_abstract: Under global warming, compound extreme events threaten ecosystems and socio-economic systems more than individual extremes. As a typical arid and semi-arid region, Northwest China has witnessed continuous increases in concurrent summer hot and drought conditions, threatening regional water security, agriculture and ecological stability. Based on observation and reanalysis data since 1961, this paper reviews recent progress on the definition, spatiotemporal variation and formation mechanisms of Summer Compound Hot-Drought Extreme Events (CHDEE) in Northwest China. Results show that the fusion scheme of daily drought and heatwave indicators, as well as the Copula joint probability framework, perform well in regional CHDEE detection. CHDEE frequency has increased significantly, with a pronounced acceleration since the late 1990s. Spatially, CHDEE show a pattern of high values in the west and low values in the east. Affected areas expand from the arid core to the northern margins and southern high-altitude regions. CHDEE are controlled by multi-scale factors: the westerly circulation, the East Asian summer monsoon and the thermal forcing of the Tibetan Plateau. The positive soil moisture–temperature feedback is the key amplification mechanism. Current studies still lack unified definitions, and the mechanisms over complex terrain remain unclear. Future work should strengthen multi-source data fusion and develop physics-informed AI prediction methods.

paper_title: Organic Residues and Cultural Memory: A Systematic Review of Archaeochemical Evidence in Reconstructing Ancient Foodways and Ritual Practices
paper_abstract: Archaeochemical investigations of organic residues have significantly advanced the reconstruction of ancient lifeways by providing molecular evidence of subsistence strategies, ritual behavior, technological practices, and socio-symbolic systems. This study presents a systematic review of archaeochemical scholarship published between 2010 and 2024, synthesizing empirical findings from forty-five peer-reviewed studies retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Guided by PRISMA 2020 protocols, the review evaluates archaeological materials analyzed, analytical techniques employed, residue categories identified, and interpretive frameworks linking biomolecular signatures to cultural memory and religious practice. The findings demonstrate the methodological dominance of chromatographic and spectrometric approaches, particularly gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry, isotope ratio mass spectrometry, and spectroscopic screening techniques. Lipid biomarkers remain foundational for reconstructing subsistence systems and dietary transitions, while increasing use of proteomic and isotopic analyses has expanded interpretive capacity toward ritual consumption practices, technological knowledge transmission, and spatial organization of domestic activities. Organic compounds such as fatty acids, fermentation markers, terpenoids, nicotine alkaloids, and resinous substances emerge as key proxies for interpreting culinary traditions, ceremonial behavior, and symbolic technological practices. The review highlights a disciplinary shift toward multi-proxy analytical integration and micro-contextual approaches that enhance the reliability of cultural reconstruction. The synthesis suggests that organic residues may be interpreted as biochemical indicators of repeated cultural practices preserved within archaeological materials. Future research directions include the development of comparative residue databases, high-resolution analytical techniques, and interdisciplinary collaboration to support more holistic reconstructions of ancient socio-cultural systems.

paper_title: Does Depression Phenotype Predict Antidepressant Response? A Transdiagnostic Review of Phenotype-Specific Antidepressant Efficacy
paper_abstract: Major depressive disorder is one of the most prevalent and disabling conditions worldwide, yet fewer than one-third of patients achieve remission with the first antidepressant prescribed. The clinical phenotypes codified across successive editions of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) — melancholic, atypical, anxious, and psychotic forms of depression — were proposed, in part, because they were thought to predict differential response to specific drug classes. This narrative review evaluates the evidence for phenotype-specific antidepressant efficacy across the full depressive spectrum, including treatment-resistant depression as a longitudinal phenotype and the transdiagnostic reformulations advanced by the Research Domain Criteria initiative. Historical controlled trials demonstrated genuine but circumscribed phenotype–drug interactions, most notably the preferential response of atypical depression to monoamine oxidase inhibitors relative to tricyclic antidepressants. However, contemporary large-scale effectiveness data from the Sequenced Treatment Alternatives to Relieve Depression (STAR*D) and the International Study to Predict Optimized Treatment in Depression (iSPOT-D) trials do not support subtype-based antidepressant selection. Much of the apparent predictive value of melancholic status is confounded by illness severity and placebo responsiveness, while data-driven re-analyses have failed to biologically validate the DSM-defined subtypes. Anxious depression and treatment-resistant depression robustly identify poorer outcomes but do not yet point clinicians toward specific drug classes. Weighing the totality of evidence, categorical depression phenotypes have limited utility in predicting antidepressant response; the most clinically reproducible signal is severity-dependent drug–placebo separation, and the most promising route to precision prescribing lies in transdiagnostic, multimodal biosignatures and machine-learning approaches.

paper_title: Comparing GenAI to Machine Learning and Manual Review for eDiscovery
paper_abstract: Keeling et al. [Keeling2026Generative] report on a case study recently conducted by Redgrave LLP in which they assert that Relativity's Generative AI Review tool (aiR) achieved 88% recall while Relativity Assisted Learning (RAL), its machine-learning tool, achieved 64% recall. These results are not comparable because the methods employed have different objectives, because of inter-assessor disagreement, and because they represent different recall-precision and cost-benefit trade-offs. Our analysis of the Redgrave data indicates that, when these differences are taken into account, aiR and manual review are comparable. Furthermore, established machine-learning models employing Continuous Active Learning (CAL) show state-of-the-art effectiveness, and superior efficiency, when trained only on a sample of 2,000 first-pass-reviewer responsiveness determinations.

paper_title: Differential Privacy Protected Preference Alignment on Survey Derived Data
paper_abstract: Preference alignment enables language models to better reflect human values, but the preference data contains sensitive information, especially when derived from surveys about political beliefs, social norms, religion, gender attitudes, and cultural values. This paper studies privacy-preserving alignment on questionnaire-derived data from the World Values Survey, where supervision takes the form of ordinal labels rather than standard pairwise rankings. Existing efforts mainly focus on general privacy protections upon model training, while data-specific methods for survey data remain unexplored. We first show the vulnerability of aligned models, then formulate the task as rating prediction and introduce label differential privacy. Building on this formulation, we construct a differential private pipeline utilizing three privacy mechanisms: randomized response, exponential mechanism, and DP-SGD. Experiments show that simple label-level mechanisms outperform gradient-level methods, and proper aggregation function for preprocessing also make large contribution. The new fine-grained private comparison motivates explorations toward language model alignment with formal privacy guarantees.

paper_title: A Survey of Flow Matching in Reinforcement Learning
paper_abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a principled and efficient generative modeling framework for reinforcement learning (RL), enabling expressive, multimodal policy parameterizations via deterministic probability transport. Compared to diffusion-based policies that rely on stochastic denoising chains, FM uses sampling based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with learned velocity fields, which can substantially reduce inference latency and simplify the incorporation of RL objectives. As research in flow-based RL rapidly accelerates across offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment, the literature has become highly fragmented. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy of flow-matching approaches in reinforcement learning. We organize the literature along two axes: the target distribution being modeled (e.g., action policies, value critics, transition dynamics) and the mechanism of RL signal integration (e.g., energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization). Furthermore, we survey emerging frontiers such as discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, provide a systematic comparative analysis against Gaussian and diffusion baselines, and outline critical open problems. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational roadmap for the next generation of generative reinforcement learning and alignment.
